messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 74
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Combat Pilot
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Touch): Physical touch, Offender Cues: Seeing the offender, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me, Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Harold Metzger is a 74-year-old widowed man who spent the better part of four decades as a combat pilot, a career defined by precision, controlled aggression, and an unwavering capacity to manage threat from the cockpit of a machine traveling at lethal speed. He is accustomed to danger arriving from the outside, from the environment, from an enemy he could see on radar or in the sky ahead. Nothing in that career prepared him for what happened inside his own home.

Following the death of his wife of thirty-one years, Harold entered a period of profound grief and, after some years of solitude, began a relationship with a woman he met through a veterans' social group. The relationship moved quickly, and within months she had moved into his home. What began as companionship gradually became something he struggled to name. She drank heavily, and when she drank, her personality shifted in ways that were, at first, unpredictable, and then, over time, entirely predictable. The smell of alcohol on her breath became a reliable prelude. On the nights that are most vivid to him now, she would come close — her hand on his arm, or gripping his wrist — and the physical contact that might have signaled affection instead preceded explosions of rage and, eventually, violence. She struck him on multiple occasions, once badly enough that he required medical attention he sought under a false explanation. He stayed far longer than he now understands, in part because he had come to believe that a man with his history — a man who had flown through anti-aircraft fire — had no right to name what was happening to him as something he could not handle.

The relationship ended approximately eighteen months ago when she was removed from his home following a particularly severe incident. But Harold has found that her departure did not restore the life he had before. In the weeks that followed, he noticed that the smell of alcohol — a neighbor's wine at a dinner party, the bar section of a restaurant, even hand sanitizer on certain days — produced an immediate and overwhelming physical response: his heart rate spiked, his hands went cold, and he felt a nauseating certainty that something was about to go wrong. He began organizing his life around avoiding these moments. He declined social invitations. He stopped going to his regular veterans' lunch because one of the men there drank beer with the meal.

Physical touch became its own territory of difficulty. When his daughter embraced him at Christmas, he felt his body go rigid in a way he could not explain to her and has not tried to. He has since kept even his children at a careful distance, finding reasons not to visit, keeping phone calls pleasant but brief. He has come to believe that closeness of any kind carries a cost he is no longer willing to pay, though he would not put it in those terms. He would say only that he prefers his own company.

At night, Harold does not sleep easily. He lies in the dark with a quality of alertness that feels less like wakefulness than like a combat readiness he cannot stand down from, his attention moving through the sounds of the house. He has not allowed himself to feel angry about what was done to him — anger, in his private accounting, is a loss of control he associates with her, not with himself — and so whatever lives beneath that suppression has no outlet he permits. He remains watchful during the day as well, tracking the movements of people around him in public spaces with an attention that exhausts him.

What finally brought Harold to seek help was not a crisis but an accumulation. His daughter told him plainly that she felt she had lost him. He sat with that for several weeks before making the appointment. He arrived at the intake session composed and precise in his language, describing his symptoms the way he might file a maintenance report. What he is most afraid of is that the clinician will not take him seriously. What he is most hoping for, though he has not said this aloud, is that someone will.
